title: A dense normal open in an integral finite-type scheme
statement:
Every integral finite-type scheme over a field has a nonempty
open subscheme
which is normal.

proof.text: Because X is integral and nonempty, choose a nonempty affine open U = Spec B. The ring B is a domain and has fraction field K = Frac B. Form the integral closure C of B in K, which is the affine chart of the normalization in [def-fin-normalization-extension]. By [lem-fin-normalization-extension-finite] (the finite-extension case with L = K), C is a finite B-module.

source.place: ## Proof, first sentence through 'the integral closure C is a finite B-module'

proof.text: Choose finite B-module generators c_1, ..., c_r of C and write each c_i as a fraction a_i/s_i in K with a_i,s_i in B and s_i nonzero. Let b = s_1 ... s_r, so b is nonzero. After localizing at b, every generator c_i belongs to B_b, hence C_b is contained in B_b. The reverse inclusion is tautological, so C_b = B_b. This is the common-denominator argument from the blueprint, written using the finite module generators.

source.place: ## Proof, 'Express its finitely many module generators as fractions ... A common nonzero denominator b gives C_b = B_b'

proof.text: The integral closure C of the domain B in its finite field extension K is a normal domain with fraction field K by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-finite-extension-normal]. Since b is nonzero, localization preserves normality by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-normal-domain], so B_b = C_b is a normal domain. Therefore Spec(B_b) is a normal open subscheme of X.

source.place: ## Proof, 'Since the integral closure is integrally closed and localization preserves this property, B_b is a normal domain'

proof.text: The principal open D(b) = Spec(B_b) is nonempty because b is nonzero in the domain B. It is dense in X because every nonempty open of an integral scheme is dense. Hence this normal open is the required nonempty dense normal open subscheme.
